query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Even in a nominally single‐phase high-entropy alloy, service-like cyclic loading at elevated temperatures locally promotes stress-assisted diffusion that triggers short-range ordering and the nucleation of brittle, ordered phases (e.g., B2 or similar intermetallic clusters) along high-stress regions such as grain boundaries or dislocation channels, ultimately degrading toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase HEA (e.g., a random solid solution with a uniform FCC or BCC structure) with no pre-existing brittle intergranular precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled cyclic or sustained near-yield loading at a temperature near the upper end of its service window.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant intermediate to high temperatures and mechanical stress levels that promote enhanced atomic mobility (but below temperatures that cause full grain coarsening) while maintaining the overall single-phase structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized regions of stress-induced short-range ordering and nanoscale formation of brittle ordered phases (e.g., B2 clusters) at grain boundaries or along dislocation slip bands.
generation.mechanism: Under cyclic or high static loads at elevated temperatures, stress-assisted diffusion allows subtle compositional fluctuations. These fluctuations drive local ordering, which leads to the nucleation of intermetallic-like precipitates in regions of high stress concentration. Such nanoclusters, even if limited in spatial extent, act as embrittling sites that impair the alloy’s overall toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an unloaded or lower-temperature baseline, the cyclically loaded sample will exhibit a measurable drop in toughness (e.g., lower fracture strain or increased brittleness) accompanied by microstructural evidence (via TEM or APT) of newly formed, nanoscale ordered regions at grain boundaries or within deformed regions.
generation.baseline: The same HEA kept in an unloaded or low-temperature condition that maintains a uniform single-phase structure with high toughness.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be active in service conditions where temperature is high enough to activate diffusion (but not so high as to induce conventional coarsening or complete phase separation) and under stresses that approach but do not exceed the yield limit; at very low temperature or under very low stresses, the alloy should retain its initial toughness.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of the ordering process, the critical stress and temperature thresholds, and the extent/size distribution of the embrittling clusters may vary with specific alloy composition and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nearly identical HEA samples. Subject one set to cyclic mechanical loading at a temperature close to the alloy’s upper service limit for an extended period (simulating service conditions), while keeping the other set as an unloaded control maintained at the same temperature. Post-treatment, perform mechanical testing to assess toughness and detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM, atom probe tomography, or high-resolution X-ray diffraction) to detect any emergence of ordered, brittle phases.
measurements: Fracture toughness and ductility (via tensile tests)
Microstructural mapping of grain boundaries and deformation zones (via TEM or APT)
Phase identification to detect any nanoscale ordered clusters (e.g., B2 phase signatures)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the loaded samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in toughness relative to the baseline control and if no localized short-range ordered or brittle phases are detectable in high-stress regions, then the hypothesis that stress-assisted local ordering is responsible for toughness degradation in the single-phase HEA is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.
